title: Switching branches with uncommitted work: carried, blocked, or stashed
summary: Sometimes git carries your edits to the new branch. Sometimes it refuses point-blank. Learn which happens when, and the three ways out.
mental_model: Uncommitted changes live outside any branch. Git carries them across a switch when the file is identical on both branches, and refuses when switching would have to overwrite your edit. The refusal is protection, not an obstacle.

commit.message: Tune the pump for the new impeller

steps.title: Edit a file that is the same on both branches
steps.why: app.py is identical on main and the feature branch, so nothing about switching would need to overwrite your edit.
steps.expect: The switch succeeds and your edit came with you. Uncommitted work belongs to you, not to a branch.

steps.title: Go back, and now edit a file that differs
steps.why: pump.py has different content on each branch. Editing it on main creates a genuine conflict of interest: switching would have to throw your edit away to install the branch's version.
steps.expect: error: Your local changes would be overwritten. Exit code 1 — git just saved your work.

steps.title: Way out 1 — stash it
steps.why: Stash takes your uncommitted changes off the working tree and records them separately. The tree becomes clean, the switch succeeds, and your edit is retrievable at any time.
commands: git stash push -m "wip: pump rpm experiment"
steps.expect: Clean tree, successful switch, one entry in the stash list.

steps.title: Get it back on the branch where it belongs
steps.why: Stashes are not tied to a branch — you can pop one anywhere. Here we go back to main and restore it, which is the common case: you stashed only to move, not to abandon.
steps.expect: RPM = 1400 is back on main, and the stash list is empty.

steps.title: Way out 2 — commit it, even roughly
steps.why: A WIP commit is cheap and completely reversible with `reset --soft`. On a branch nobody else pulls, this is often better than stashing: it survives crashes and shows up in the reflog.
steps.expect: The switch is now trivial, because there is nothing uncommitted.

steps.title: Undo the WIP commit, keeping the work
steps.why: `reset --soft HEAD~1` removes the commit and leaves everything staged. This is the standard pattern: commit to move safely, then unwind the commit when you are ready to do the work properly.

verify.label: the WIP commit is gone but the change survives

steps.title: Way out 3 — take the changes with you deliberately
steps.why: `switch -m` performs a three-way merge of your uncommitted changes into the target branch. It works, and it can produce conflict markers in an uncommitted file — powerful, but the one to reach for last.
steps.expect: Git merges your edit into the branch's version rather than refusing.

verify.label: nothing was left abandoned in the stash
verify.hint: git stash pop to bring it back

verify.label: no WIP commit was left in history
verify.hint: git reset --soft HEAD~1 unwinds it while keeping the change

verify.label: the feature branch is untouched by all of this

pitfalls: Carried changes are not 'on' the new branch — they are uncommitted. Commit them on the wrong branch and you have made a mess that needs cherry-pick to fix.
`git stash` does not include untracked files by default. Use `-u`, or your new file stays behind and confuses you on the other branch.
`git switch -m` can leave conflict markers in files that are not committed anywhere. If it goes wrong, `git checkout --merge` cannot save you — there is no commit to go back to.
`git switch --discard-changes` exists and does exactly what it says. It is the `reset --hard` of switching.
cheatsheet: carries edits when it safely can, refuses when it cannot
park uncommitted work with a label
unwind a WIP commit, keep the changes
merge uncommitted changes into the target branch
throw the edits away and go
